rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Mirror formula (Cartesian, sign convention applied): $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$.
Magnification: $m = \frac{h'}{h} = -\frac{v}{u}$.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ The mirror formula is $1/f = 1/v - 1/u$. ✅ The correct formula is $1/f = 1/u + 1/v$ (with sign convention applied). The lens formula $1/f = 1/v - 1/u$ looks similar but has a different sign convention.  ·  ❌ $f = R$ for spherical mirrors. ✅ The focal length is HALF the radius of curvature: $f = R/2$. The focus is midway between the pole and the center of curvature.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ Object distance $u$ is always positive. ✅ By the New Cartesian convention, object distance is NEGATIVE (measured against the direction of incident light). $u < 0$ for real objects in front of the mirror.  ·  ❌ The mirror formula works for all rays, not just paraxial ones. ✅ The formula is derived using the paraxial approximation (small angles). For rays far from the axis, spherical aberration causes deviations. The formula is accurate only for mirrors with small aperture relative to $R$.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Apply the Cartesian sign convention first (distances measured from the pole, along the incident light positive) — with it one formula serves concave and convex mirrors.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The mirror formula was first derived by Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, 965–1040 CE) using geometric methods, over 500 years before it was independently rediscovered by European scientists.  ·  The relation $f = R/2$ holds exactly for paraxial rays but breaks down for wide-aperture mirrors due to spherical aberration. Parabolic mirrors eliminate this aberration and are used in telescopes.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Mirror formula.** For a spherical mirror, object distance u, image distance v and focal length f satisfy 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.  ·  **Focal length.** The focal length is half the radius of curvature, f = R/2; it is negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex mirror under the Cartesian sign convention.  ·  **Magnification.** Linear magnification m = −v/u = h'/h; a negative value means a real inverted image and a positive value a virtual erect one.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Mirror formula and other topics  ·  ❌ A convex mirror can produce a real image. ✅ A convex mirror ALWAYS produces a virtual image. Its reflected rays always diverge and never actually converge to form a real image.  ·  ❌ Magnification $m = v/u$ (without the negative sign). ✅ The correct formula is $m = -v/u$. The negative sign is essential: it ensures that real images (where $v$ and $u$ have opposite signs) give negative magnification (inverted).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The image distance $v$ is positive for real images in the New Cartesian convention. ✅ In the New Cartesian convention, $v$ is NEGATIVE for real images (in front of the mirror, opposite to incident light direction). $v$ is POSITIVE for virtual images (behind the mirror).  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Mirror formula  ·  Note 4: Remember the units and dimensions involved in Mirror formula
